subject: English
description: Conditional sentences — zero, first, second, third type; mixed conditionals; if-clauses; unless, provided that, in case.

questions.stem: Identify the type: 'If you heat ice, it melts.'
questions.explanation: ZERO CONDITIONAL: 'If + present simple, present simple.' Used for SCIENTIFIC FACTS, GENERAL TRUTHS, automatic consequences. Example: 'If you heat ice, it melts.' EVERY time you heat ice, it melts — universal truth. STRUCTURE: IF + V1 (present simple), V1 (present simple). 'When' can replace 'if' in zero conditional with the same meaning ('When you heat ice, it melts'). FOUR MAIN CONDITIONALS: (0) ZERO — facts: If + present, present. 'If you mix red and blue, you get purple.' (1) FIRST — real future: If + present, will + V1. 'If it rains, I will stay home.' (2) SECOND — unreal/hypothetical present/future: If + past, would + V1. 'If I were rich, I would travel.' (3) THIRD — unreal past: If + past perfect, would have + V3. 'If I had studied, I would have passed.' MIXED — combinations of past unreal cause + present unreal effect: 'If I had studied harder, I would be a doctor now.' KEY EXAM TRAP: 'will' NEVER goes in the IF-CLAUSE in standard conditionals. PYQ FREQUENCY: conditionals appear in SSC CGL, IBPS PO English 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'If it ___ tomorrow, we will cancel the picnic.'
questions.explanation: FIRST CONDITIONAL: refers to REAL/POSSIBLE FUTURE situations. STRUCTURE: 'If + PRESENT SIMPLE, WILL + base verb'. So 'If it RAINS tomorrow, we WILL cancel the picnic.' KEY ERROR (very common): students write 'If it WILL RAIN' — INCORRECT. The IF-CLAUSE uses present tense even though it refers to the future. Reason: English uses present-tense in the if-clause to describe the FUTURE CONDITION; 'will' is reserved for the result-clause. EXCEPTIONS — 'will' CAN appear in if-clause when: (a) Polite request: 'If you WILL wait here, I'll get the manager.' (b) Stress on willingness: 'If you WILL NOT cooperate, we'll have to fire you.' But these are special, NOT standard conditional. ALSO ACCEPTABLE: 'might', 'may', 'can', 'should', 'shall' in result-clause: 'If it rains, I MIGHT stay home' (less certain than 'will stay home'). FIRST CONDITIONAL is for FUTURE possibilities you consider REAL. SECOND CONDITIONAL ('If I were you, I would not go') is for HYPOTHETICAL/UNREAL situations. PYQ FREQUENCY: first vs second conditional confusion is a top SSC CGL, IBPS PO English MCQ — 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'If I ___ a millionaire, I would travel the world.'
questions.explanation: SECOND CONDITIONAL: hypothetical/unreal PRESENT or FUTURE. STRUCTURE: 'If + past simple, would + base verb'. Special case: SUBJUNCTIVE — 'were' is used (instead of 'was') for ALL persons in formal English with the verb 'BE'. So 'If I WERE a millionaire' (NOT 'If I WAS a millionaire' in formal usage). 'If he WERE here, he would help.' PURPOSE OF SUBJUNCTIVE: emphasizes that the situation is HYPOTHETICAL — opposite of reality. INFORMAL ENGLISH allows 'was': 'If I was rich, I'd buy a house' — acceptable in casual speech but marked DOWN in formal exams. KEY EXAM PATTERN: 'If I were' = correct in SSC CGL, IBPS PO English-section. EXTENSION TO PHRASES: 'If I were you, I would...' (advice-giving formula); 'I wish I were taller' (regret/desire); 'It's time you were leaving' (suggestion). MIXED CONDITIONAL: 'If I had studied harder (past), I would be successful now (present)' — combines third-conditional cause + second-conditional effect. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'were' vs 'was' in conditionals is a top SSC, IBPS English MCQ — 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Pick the correct form: 'If I had known earlier, I ___ helped you.'
questions.explanation: THIRD CONDITIONAL: UNREAL PAST — situations that DIDN'T happen. STRUCTURE: 'If + past perfect (had + V3), would have + V3'. So 'If I HAD KNOWN, I WOULD HAVE HELPED you' = I didn't know, so I didn't help. The past is fixed; this clause expresses REGRET or COUNTERFACTUAL musing. KEY VERB FORMS: PAST PERFECT (had + V3) in if-clause; MODAL PERFECT (would/could/might + have + V3) in result-clause. EXAMPLES: (1) 'If she had studied, she would have passed' (regret about exam failure). (2) 'If I had taken the umbrella, I wouldn't have got wet' (mixed positive in if + negative in result). (3) 'If they had left earlier, they could have caught the train' (could expresses missed possibility). USE: expressing REGRET, CRITICISM, COUNTERFACTUAL ANALYSIS — common in personal reflection, journalism, political analysis. EXAM TRAP: students miss the 'have' in the result-clause: 'I would helped' — INCORRECT; needs 'I would HAVE helped'. PYQ FREQUENCY: third conditional structure in SSC CGL, IBPS PO English — 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Choose the right form: 'UNLESS you study hard, you ___ pass.'
questions.explanation: 'UNLESS' = 'IF NOT'. So 'Unless you study hard' = 'If you don't study hard'. The structure follows FIRST CONDITIONAL: 'If you don't study hard, you WILL NOT pass' → 'Unless you study hard, you WILL NOT pass'. Same logic: present in unless-clause, will in result-clause. KEY: unless ALREADY contains the negative meaning, so DON'T add another negative in the unless-clause. WRONG: 'Unless you don't study hard, you will pass' — DOUBLE NEGATIVE, incorrect. CORRECT: 'Unless you study hard, you will fail.' EQUIVALENTS: 'unless' ≈ 'if...not' or 'except if'. 'I won't go unless you come' = 'I won't go if you don't come' = 'I will go ONLY IF you come'. RELATED CONDITIONALS: (1) 'PROVIDED THAT' / 'AS LONG AS' = 'IF', with emphasis on condition: 'You can stay provided that you pay rent'. (2) 'IN CASE' = for precaution: 'Take an umbrella in case it rains' (= because it might rain). (3) 'OTHERWISE' = 'or else': 'Hurry up, otherwise we'll be late'. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'unless' usage is a top SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO MCQ — 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Identify the conditional: 'If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor today.'
questions.explanation: MIXED CONDITIONAL — combines TWO types in one sentence. STRUCTURE: 'If + past perfect (3rd conditional cause), would + V1 (2nd conditional effect)'. EXAMPLE breakdown: 'If I HAD STUDIED medicine [past unreal, didn't happen], I WOULD BE a doctor today [present unreal effect]'. The PAST didn't happen, hence the PRESENT consequence is also unreal. PURE 3RD CONDITIONAL would have been: 'If I had studied medicine, I would have been a doctor' (entirely past — sounds odd because being a doctor is a present-state implication). PURE 2ND CONDITIONAL: 'If I studied medicine, I would be a doctor' (hypothetical present-future, ignoring real past). MIXED IS GOOD when CAUSE is past + EFFECT is present. ANOTHER VARIANT: 'If she WERE more careful (present unreal), she WOULD HAVE PASSED the exam (past hypothetical)' — present-cause + past-effect mix. USAGE: mixed conditionals are common in REGRET expressions and counterfactual analysis: 'If you'd called me yesterday, I wouldn't be in this mess now.' PYQ FREQUENCY: mixed conditionals are advanced English — 1 per CAT, 1 per IBPS PO Mains, occasional SSC CGL Tier 2.

questions.stem: Pick the correct form: 'I wish I ___ taller. (expressing regret)'
questions.explanation: WISHES — closely related to second conditional structurally. PATTERN: 'I wish + past simple' for PRESENT REGRET/UNREAL DESIRE: 'I wish I WERE taller' (I'm not, but I want to be). 'I wish I HAD a car' (don't have one). 'I wish I COULD speak French' (can't). FOR PAST REGRETS: 'I wish + past perfect' (i.e., 'had + V3'): 'I wish I HAD STUDIED harder' (didn't, regret it now). FOR ANNOYING SITUATIONS: 'I wish + would + V1': 'I wish you would stop interrupting' (criticism). 'IF ONLY' is a stronger form: 'If only I were rich!' (more emphatic than 'I wish'). KEY: 'WERE' is used for ALL persons (I, you, he, she, it, we, they) in formal English with 'wish' or '2nd conditional' — this is the SUBJUNCTIVE MOOD. Informal English allows 'was' but exams prefer 'were'. WHY THIS RULE: signals that the statement is COUNTERFACTUAL, not historical. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'I wish I were' constructions in SSC CGL, IBPS PO English — 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests subjunctive-mood mastery; rewards formal-English discipline.
